items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, October 2026 Zillow forecasts 2.8% rent inflation, 3.3% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on October 27, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Friday, November 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to stay elevated through the end of the year and into 2027. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 up around 3.1% and OER up near 3.4%. September’s reading on Owners’ Equivalent rates showed growth at the upper end of expectations, but this is unlikely to be the start of a great rise. Shelter disinflation has effectively plateaued in the near-term. New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, putting a damper on the declines in measured housing inflation. Forecasts for on-market rents have been revised higher for the past few months. Current trends suggest that by year-end, the annual rate of growth will be roughly equal between new-lease rents and CPI rents, keeping a floor under inflation. items.title: New Home Sales Declined in September as Builders Focused on Inventory Management
items.description: New Home Sales Declined in September as Builders Focused on Inventory Management Written by Kenny Lee on October 27, 2026 What happened New home sales fell slightly by 0.6% to 676 thousand SAAR in September, essentially holding firm at 680 thousand in August but 5.3% below a year ago. The median price of new homes sold declined 3.9% from a year ago, to $400,400. As homebuilders delay new construction, the number of new homes on the market fell 2.3% year over year to 476 thousand homes in September — marking the 11th consecutive month of annual decline. Inventory adjustment has been a counterbalance to cooler inventory. At the latest sales pace, it would take about 8.4 months to clear the inventory, up slightly from 8.2 months a year ago. Smaller and more affordable units constituted a larger share of total sales, with 70% of homes selling below $500,000 in September. As elevated mortgage rates keep buyers on the sidelines, the share will likely continue to rise. By comparison, 66% of new homes sold were below this price point in September last year. Inventory management would remain the number one priority for builders For builders, the ongoing shift toward smaller homes was prudent and necessary. While mortgage rates soared above 7% in September, homebuilders have been navigating elevated rates, in addition to their wild swings, for a while. Builders will remain focused on inventory management, especially as competition from the resale market increases. Zillow’s September report shows resale inventory rose 2.5% year over year, marking the 34th consecutive month of annual gains. In addition, 27.4% of sellers reduced asking prices as they adapt to shifting buyer demand. Building smaller homes is a win-win for both buyers and builders. For buyers, a lower entry point helps them navigate the challenging affordability landscape. For builders, they can keep their inventory moving even as buyers see more options in the resale market. items.title: FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged
items.description: Economic Coverage FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged By Danielle Hale Oct 28, 2026 The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC), the rate-setting body that meets roughly eight times per year, left the Federal Funds rate unchanged at its October meeting in a target range of 3.75 to 4.0 percent. This hold follows a 25 basis point hike in September, and was supported by 10 of the 12 voting members. Two voters, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented, because they preferred to raise the rate by a quarter percentage point instead of holding. Even though the Fed left its policy rate unchanged in October, the market is anticipating another 2 to 3 hikes over the next 6 to 8 months which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5 to 4.75 percent. This is slightly above the high-end of Fed funds rate projections made in September, and would position the Fed funds rate roughly halfway between its December 2025 to September 2026 low of 3.5 to 3.75 percent and its 5.25 to 5.5 percent prior peak. While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected. Why further rate hikes are expected Since the September FOMC meeting, when the Fed pushed its rate 25 basis points higher, companies slowed hiring and summer job gains were revised down by 60,000 jobs . The unemployment rate remains relatively stable at 4.2 percent and layoffs are low, but the labor market is less dynamic than is ideal. Meanwhile, inflation surprised to the upside, with the CPI rising 0.6% in September, bringing the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% as the cost of gas and energy rose sharply. Energy was not the only driver, however, and core CPI, which strips out the cost of food and energy, rose 2.6% in September. Taken together, these indicators suggest that the Fed is likely to continue its focus on inflation, which will likely warrant additional rate hikes. What this means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers Investors have made a round-trip in risk pricing since just before the September Fed meeting. The 10-year yield rose from just under 5 percent to more than 5.3 percent before dipping just under 5 percent in recent days, while mortgage rates climbed from just below 7 percent to more than 7.4 percent. Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record according to the National Association of Realtors as buyers and sellers have largely disengaged with the housing market for now. In August and September, existing-home sales dropped below a 4 million sales pace, and are likely to remain low through the rest of the year. Home shoppers shopping in this environment can still set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit, making a higher down payment, and, most importantly, shopping around for a mortgage. Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility and rate-proof their home shopping budget by testing out a range of possible mortgage rates so they’ll be prepared to react.

items.title: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month
items.description: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Oct 29, 2026 Highlights In 2026Q3, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County registered at $2,554,—down $96, or 3.6%, from a year earlier. The median asking rent for 0-2 bedrooms in L.A. County was $2,239, reflecting a decline of $88 (-3.8%) from the previous year. Meanwhile, rent for 3+ bedroom units dropped by $70 (-1.9%) compared to 2025Q3, standing at $3,571. For renters in L.A. County : Buying costs far more than renting. In 2026Q3, a median-priced home cost $4,716 more a month than renting one, nearly 185% higher, even though the monthly buying cost fell about 2% as home prices dropped. Mortgage rates above 7% could erase that relief. At 7%, the same home would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the savings from lower prices In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for all rental properties listed on Realtor.com in Los Angeles County was $2,554, a decline of $96, or 3.6%, compared with a year ago. While the county experienced a temporary dip in rents during the pandemic, asking rents quickly rebounded to pre-pandemic levels and peaked in the summer of 2022. Since then, a surge in new multifamily construction has put sustained downward pressure on rent. In the most recent quarter, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County was $340, or 11.7%, below its 2022 peak. In addition, Los Angeles County renters are overwhelmingly local. In the third quarter of 2026, more than half (61.3%) of online traffic to L.A. County rental listings originated from within the county, with an additional 15.5% coming from elsewhere in California. Out-of-state renters accounted for 19.8% of traffic, while international traffic represented 3.4%. Breaking down by bedroom type, the median asking rent for 0-2 bedroom units in Los Angeles County was $2,239 in 2026Q3, a decline of $88 or 3.8%, from a year ago. Larger units with three or more bedrooms saw a comparatively modest softening, with a median asking rent of $3,571 — down $70, or 1.9%, year-over-year. The steeper rent decline among smaller units suggests renters in that segment are experiencing greater pricing relief. The surge in ADUs across Los Angeles County may partially explain this trend. As those permitted units complete construction — typically requiring 6 to 18 months from permit to occupancy — a growing wave of new small rental units has been entering the market, adding downward price pressure concentrated in the smaller unit segment. Consistent with the broader L.A. County trend, rents in the City of Los Angeles have been on a downward trajectory since peaking in the summer of 2022. While the current median remains $158, or 5.5%, above pre-pandemic levels, renters today are saving $363 per month, or 11.8%, compared to the 2022 peak, translating to $4,356 in annual savings. Nevertheless, in order to afford a typical home in the city of Los Angeles, a minimum annual income of $108,320 is required— 22.1% higher than the city's estimated median household income of $88,730 1 High mortgage rates squeeze renters hoping to buy Renters may be catching a break, but for most renters who want to become homeowners in L.A. County, homeownership remains out of reach. On top of that, with mortgage rates now above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push homeownership even further out of reach for renters who want to buy. In 2026Q3, buying a typical home in L.A. County costs $4,716 more per month than renting one. Buying got slightly cheaper over the past year because home prices fell, even as mortgage rates rose. The median listing price dropped 3.2% to $970,000 over the past year, which more than offset a small increase in the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, from 6.57% to 6.68%. As a result, the estimated monthly cost of buying a median-priced home fell about 2.1%, or $159, from a year earlier, to $7,270. But that relief may not last. Rates surpassed 7% in late-September and remain well- above this mark. At 7%, the same home price would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the monthly payment savings from lower prices. Methodology To determine the monthly cost of buying a home, we find the median listing price for homes in Los Angeles County. As first-time homebuyers plan lower down payments, we assume a 10% down payment and use the 30-year fixed mortgage rate during the quarter to calculate a monthly mortgage payment. We also include the HOA fees, taxes, and homeowners insurance as part of the costs. L.A. rental data as of 2026Q3 for all units advertised for rent on Realtor.com®. Rental units include apartments as well as private rentals (condos, townhomes, single-family homes). We use rental sources that reliably report data each month within L.A. county. To calculate the median asking rent for each quarter, we first obtain the median asking rent for each month within that quarter and then take the average of the three months. items.title: Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3
items.description: Economic Coverage , Homeownership Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3 By Hannah Jones Oct 28, 2026 2026 Q3 Homeownership and Housing Vacancy Key Takeaways Homeownership rate holds steady. The U.S. homeownership rate was 65.5% in Q3 2026, statistically unchanged from both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). The rate continues to plateau in a narrow low-to-mid-65% band, with affordability pressures and limited supply showing little sign of easing their grip on the market. Homeowner vacancy remains low and steady. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3, virtually unchanged from both the prior quarter and a year earlier. Rental vacancy reaches its highest level in over a decade. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6%, up both quarter-over-quarter (7.3%) and year-over-year (7.1%), its highest level since 2014. Renting remains a critical pressure valve, though conditions vary by geography. With a national rental vacancy rate of 7.6%, rental markets continue to offer more flexibility for households unable to buy. Principal cities (8.8%) remain looser than suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%), which were statistically similar to each other. The South leads in vacancy levels, while the Northeast and West saw the clearest year-over-year shifts. The South posted the highest rental vacancy rate (9.2%) and homeowner vacancy rate (1.5%) of any region, though neither was statistically different from a year ago. Rental vacancy rose significantly in the Northeast (5.0% to 6.2%) and the West (6.0% to 6.7%). Ownership slipped among 35-to-44-year-olds, while older households gained. Homeownership among 35-to-44-year-olds fell from 61.1% to 60.1% year-over-year. Households under 35 remain the lowest at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Meanwhile, 65+ homeownership rose from 77.9% to 79.1%. Racial ownership gaps remain entrenched. Homeownership among Black households fell from 45.7% to 44.4% year-over-year, while White homeownership rose from 74.0% to 75.1%. All other groups did not see statistically significant shifts. What happened this quarter The U.S. homeownership rate held at 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, statistically unchanged compared with both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). While the rate remains within the narrow low-to-mid-65% range that has characterized the market in recent years, it continues to run well below the 2020 pandemic-era peak. Mortgage rates pushed back above 7% in late September for the first time in more than a year, which could weigh on would-be buyers heading into the fourth quarter. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3 2026, virtually the same as the previous quarter and the previous year. While homeowner vacancy remains below pre-pandemic norms, the recent pick up in inventory could mean vacancy drifts higher if demand is not sufficient to absorb supply. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6% in the third quarter, higher than both the previous quarter (7.3%) and the previous year (7.1%). With mortgage rates moving back above 7%, renting continues to stand out as a more affordable alternative to homeownership. However, climbing rental vacancy suggests that units are sitting empty as affordability pressure may discourage household formation. Vacancy was highest in principal cities (8.8%). Suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%) were lower and not statistically different from each other. Regional differences remain pronounced . The South recorded the highest rental vacancy rate at 9.2%, followed by the Midwest (7.1%), the West (6.7%), and the Northeast (6.2%). The Midwest was higher than the Northeast and statistically similar to the West, while the Northeast and West were not statistically different from each other. Of the four regions, only the Northeast (up from 5.0%) and West (up from 6.0%) saw a statistically significant year-over-year increase in rental vacancy. Rental vacancy has stalled in the South as the wave of supply has subsided . The post-pandemic construction boom flooded these markets with new supply, but as multifamily construction has slowed, vacancy growth has stalled. On the ownership side, the South again led with the highest homeowner vacancy rate at 1.5%, while the other three regions saw vacancy between 0.9% and 1.1%. The Midwest continues to stand out for its high homeownership rate, reaching 69.5% in Q3 2026, though not statistically different from a year earlier, and remains well above the South (67.2%), Northeast (62.9%), and West (60.6%). Different outcomes by race/ethnicity Homeownership rates by race and ethnicity were mixed year over year. In the third quarter, the rate for non-Hispanic White householders rose to 75.1% from 74.0%, while the rate for Asian, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander householders was statistically unchanged at 62.3%. The rate for Black householders fell to 44.4% from 45.7%, and the rate for Hispanic householders was statistically unchanged at 48.1%. The gap between the highest and lowest rates remains more than 30 percentage points, underscoring the persistence of structural barriers to ownership. Different outcomes by age Ownership among younger households remains low, while older householders saw improvement. Homeownership among those under 35 was the lowest of any age group at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Homeownership among households aged 35 to 44 fell from 61.1% in Q3 of 2025 to 60.1% in Q3 of 2026. Ownership in the 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 cohorts held steady at 70.4% and 75.4%, respectively, while the 65+ group saw a 1.2 percentage point improvement to 79.1%. Ample starter-home inventory is crucial for young homeownership, and availability varies significantly across the country .

items.title: Down Payment Assistance Could Cut the Time to Save for a Home by a Year and a Half or More
items.description: Down Payment Assistance Could Cut the Time to Save for a Home by a Year and a Half or More Nationally, a 3.5% down payment boost allows a typical buyer to save for a 10% down payment 35% faster October 28, 2026 Anushna Prakash Written by Anushna Prakash Key findings: A median-income household could save 10% down on the typical U.S. home after 4.2 years, according to Zillow’s estimates. With down payment assistance covering 3.5% of that, the time to save would be cut to 2.7 years. Moving from a 6.5% down payment to 10% on a typical U.S. home would save a buyer $1,080 per year in monthly payments. Nationally, those monthly savings would bring an additional 26,338 homes within reach for a median-income buyer. Saving 10% down on the typical U.S. home takes the median household an estimated 4.2 years, or about four years and two months. With a down payment assistance program covering 3.5% of that 10% down payment, the same household could have enough saved a year and a half sooner. The same assistance also lowers a typical buyer’s mortgage payments by $1,080 a year, putting more homes within reach. Nationally, about 26,300 more active listings would become affordable in this scenario. For this analysis, Zillow is assuming a buyer puts a total of 10% down and receives an FHA loan . However, the minimum down payment for an FHA loan is 3.5%, meaning a buyer could also use this level of assistance to cover the entirety of their down payment. Making a smaller down payment does bring up the monthly mortgage payment some, but is a viable option for a buyer with the financial means to cover the monthly payment but without the necessary savings for a down payment. Zillow research has shown that one in five renter households headed by someone ages 29 to 43 could afford the monthly cost of owning a typical home in their market with just 5% down. A 3.5% boost cuts the time to save a 10% down payment by as much as 3.2 years Nationally, a median-income household saving for a 10% down payment on a typical U.S. home needs 4.2 years. That number could be cut to 2.7 years with a 3.5% boost from down payment assistance, a difference of 1.5 years. The benefit is biggest for a buyer in some of the most expensive metro areas, led by Los Angeles, where the years to save fall from 9.1 years to 5.9 years, putting homeownership within reach more than three years sooner. Three other major California metros see gaps of more than two and a half years: San Jose (8.5 years to 5.5 years with down payment assistance), San Diego (7.9 to 5.1) and San Francisco (7.7 to 5). Pittsburgh is the only major metro area where down payment assistance does not shave at least a year off the time needed to save 10% down on a typical home. A median-income Pittsburgh household could save 10% down after 2.7 years, which would be shortened to 1.8 years with down payment assistance. Lower payments save buyers $1,080 a year, bringing more listings within budget With a 6.5% down payment and a 6.78% mortgage rate (the average rate for an FHA loan in September), the monthly payment on a $366,157 home (the typical home value in September, according to the Zillow Home Value Index) would have been $3,010, including estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. If given a 3.5% boost via down payment assistance, that same home purchase would come with a monthly payment of $2,920, a savings of $1,080 per year. The annual savings are largest in San Jose ($4,608), San Francisco ($3,396), Los Angeles ($2,880), San Diego ($2,808) and New York ($2,160). Those monthly payment savings can bring more homes within reach. Nationally, 359,434 active listings were affordable to this hypothetical buyer with 6.5% down in September, representing 25.7% of what was listed for sale. With the 3.5% down payment assistance, 26,338 more listings would have been affordable, raising the share of affordable listings to 27.6%. Receiving 3.5% in down payment assistance would have brought the most listings newly within reach in Dallas (864), Atlanta (712), Miami (558) and Washington, D.C. (555). How the numbers work For years-to-save calculations , Zillow assumes a median-income household saves 10% of its income each month. This analysis assumes a household is buying the typical home in a given metro, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index as of September 2026 . This analysis assumes a buyer is receiving an FHA loan, aligning with the down payment assistance program recently announced by Zillow Home Loans. Monthly housing costs assume a buyer purchases the typical home in a given metro, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index as of September 2026. Estimates assume a mortgage rate of 6.78%, the average for an FHA loan in September, and include estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. Homes are considered affordable if the household would spend no more than 30% of its income on the total monthly payment. items.title: HUFFMAN AREA LEADS HOUSTON'S HOTTEST COMMUNITIES WITH TRIPLE-DIGIT GROWTH
items.description: Media Contacts Brittany Aucion Director of Communications (713) 629-1900 ext.1256 Send email Isabela Ortiz Consumer Marketing Specialist (713) 629-1900 ext.1254 Send email HUFFMAN AREA LEADS HOUSTON’S HOTTEST COMMUNITIES WITH TRIPLE-DIGIT GROWTH Needville Area and Sugar Land East follow with significant gains in third quarter HOUSTON -- (October 26, 2026) -- From newly built homes to more affordable price points, buyers are finding opportunities in communities across the Greater Houston area that are seeing some of the region's biggest gains in home sales. According to HAR's latest Hottest Communities in the Houston Area report, the Huffman Area led all communities with a 166.7% year-over-year increase in home sales during the third quarter of 2026. Home sales climbed from 63 to 168 properties sold, putting the community back in the top spot after ranking second in the previous quarter. Needville Area followed with an 80.6% increase in transactions, while Sugar Land East posted a 52.9% gain. Waller (up 45.7%) and Humble Area East (up 36.7%) rounded out the top five. New construction continues to account for a significant share of sales in several of the hottest communities. Newly built homes represented 87.6% of transactions in Waller, 81.5% in Needville Area and 62.5% in the Huffman Area. Home prices varied across the top 10 communities, with seven reporting average prices below the Houston-area average of $421,311. The Huffman Area recorded an average home price of $276,515, while Needville Area averaged $335,494. "Buyers are looking for value, and these communities are showing that there are still opportunities to find it," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "New construction is helping meet that demand by offering more choices at different price points. It's encouraging to see that kind of activity across so many parts of the Houston area." The report also highlights the top-performing luxury communities in Greater Houston, where average home prices are at least $1 million. The Tanglewood Area led the luxury rankings for the third consecutive quarter, with an 84.6% year-over-year increase in home sales. Transactions rose from 13 to 24, with an average home price of $2,705,229. items.title: Why home prices and new home sales aren’t as hot as today’s reports show
items.description: Home prices were actually improving on a year-over-year basis recently, which should make you question anyone who has been saying this. Also, even though new home sales data beat estimates while mortgage rates were elevated, you should view it through the lens of a rate-buydown marketplace. The new home sales sector has been living off rate buydowns from builders, whereas the existing home sales market hasn’t. So, let's look at both reports and try to explain what is happening. Home prices From Case Shiller : The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index posted a 2.1% annual gain for August 2026, up from a 1.9% rise in the previous month. U.S. home values fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August’s 3.4% inflation ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the 2.1% home price gain. A nearly 9-percentage-point gap separated August’s strongest market (Chicago +6.7% YoY) and its weakest (Seattle -2.0% YoY), underscoring the strong regional divergence in home price trends. My home-price forecast for this year is -0.62%, as I've said in the Housing Market Tracker articles for a while, and I think it will be hard to reach in 2026. Even though mortgage rates are elevated and demand is finally taking a noticeable hit as inventory rises, I don’t think I will have enough time in 2026 to be right. Home prices have been up 1%-2% year over year every month. The Case Shiller index lags our data by a few months. Inventory actually went negative in mid-June . As we have talked about throughout the year, the year-over-year comps were going to be hard to show growth until mid-June. Then the supply-to-demand equilibrium improved as rates fell, giving us a bit more pricing power. But mortgage rates started to go above 7% in September , and the dynamic shifted. So our data is a few months ahead of the Case-Shiller index, and price growth will get hit, but keep in mind year-over-year comps are easy to beat now. Because we hardly had any price growth last year, all in all, this is still a very healthy housing market in the sense that inventory is up, price growth is cooling down and wages are outpacing home prices. That wasn't the case in 2023, when mortgage rates rose to 8% but home prices were up 6%. Home-price growth should be cooling down when the Case Shiller catches up, but as you can see now, if you wasted one second of your life on national home price crash doomers from 2012-2026, you wasted your precious time on untalented hacks. New home sales From Census : New Home Sales Sales of new single-family houses in September 2026 were at a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 676,000, according to estimates released jointly today by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development. This is 0.6 percent (±13.8 percent)* below the August 2026 rate of 680,000, and is 5.3 percent (±12.5 percent)* below the September 2025 rate of 714,000 . This is the same story I have talked about for years: the new home sales data — if you remove the COVID burst in sales and the decline from that peak — has really gone nowhere for 10 years. New home sales are still at 2019 levels, even though demand for housing is there with lower rates. In fact, if we applied the same rate profile to the existing home sales market, we would have seen growth years ago. However, I don’t believe existing home sales would be trending at 2019 levels if mortgage rates were between 4.75% and 5.75%, which is where rates are with builder buydowns. They would be higher for sure, but not at 2019 levels, as that would amount to 1 to 1.3 million more existing home sales than today’s levels. So for now, after revisions, new home sales don’t really break above 730,000 or go below 570,000 on a monthly basis; we can have a few prints above or below these levels, but we've been stuck in this sales channel for years now. One positive story going untold: builders are slowly reducing excess supply ; for housing starts to really grow, this pool needs to shrink, and new home sales need to grow. One reason housing starts aren’t even worse today is that buy-downs have kept demand at 2019 levels while builders work through excess supply. Much more work remains, but it hasn’t gotten worse even with higher rates; the question is whether this can continue into 2027 with rates above 7% and profit margins falling. Conclusion All in all, nothing too surprising with the Case-Shiller Home Price Index or new home sales data if you look at it with the same lens I do. I think some people might be surprised since rates are elevated right now and the existing home sales demand has been softening up, but again, the Case Shiller index lags, and the new home sales market is still working with the sub-6 % mortgage market world. So as long as you look at it in that context, today’s data makes a little bit more sense. Tomorrow the Federal Reserve meets and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will give his remarks. I gave a preview of this in today's episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast and tried to explain why the Fed won’t hike rates tomorrow. Related More: Home Price Index Home Sales

items.title: Las Vegas multifamily rent pressures persist despite leasing gains
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Las Vegas multifamily market report here.HighlightsLas Vegas multifamily operating conditions remain soft, with elevated vacancy, rising concessions and declining rents. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, but the improved supply-demand balance has yet to translate into rent growth.Stabilized vacancy reached 9.1% at the end of the third quarter, flat from the prior quarter but up 20 basis points from one year earlier. Vacancy remains 30 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month by the end of September, down 1.4% year over year and 0.9% lower than in the prior quarter, the second consecutive quarterly decline.Investment sales volume during the third quarter totaled roughly $209 million across five deals, with Class B properties accounting for four of the five deals. The year-to-date median sale price reached $225,900 per unit.Las Vegas multifamily market overviewLas Vegas multifamily fundamentals remain under pressure despite improved absorption and a slowdown in new deliveries in 2026. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries by roughly 650 units year to date, after trailing them by nearly 1,700 units in 2025. Absorption has already surpassed the full-year 2025 total, supported by continued job growth, while completions have slowed as fewer projects remain under construction. The recovery has been concentrated in the suburbs, where Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of that demand with less than half of the metro’s inventory. Rent growth has been slower to rebound. Asking rents remain below year-ago levels, with the steepest declines in older urban core submarkets, where vacancy is above 10%. By contrast, rents in suburban submarkets remain close to year-ago levels.Investment activity in 2026 has become concentrated in two of the suburban submarkets that are leading the leasing recovery. Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson accounted for roughly three-quarters of metro sales volume through the third quarter, up from 43% in 2025. Third-quarter activity followed the same pattern, with three of the five trades located in those two submarkets. Pricing has remained stable in Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson, with median sale prices near $250,000 per unit in both submarkets, above levels elsewhere in the metro, where recent trades have skewed toward smaller, older properties. The median price across the Las Vegas region has remained near its 2025 level, highlighting the influence of property location on pricing trends.Employment:Area employers added 21,400 jobs year over year. Year-to-date deliveries total around 2,600 units, down 23% from the same period in 2025. Roughly 6,100 units were under construction at the end of the third quarter, down more than 25% from the end of 2025, which is expected to ease supply pressure on operators heading into 2027. Six active projects in Spring Valley total more than 2,000 units.Multifamily permitting activity is regaining momentum. Developers pulled permits for 1,130 multifamily units in the third quarter, more than double the total from one year earlier.Forecast: Developers are expected to complete roughly 4,000 units in 2026, in line with both the 2025 total and the 10-year average.Vacancy:Vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1% Image Stabilized vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1%, up 20 basis points year over year. Las Vegas Strip vacancy rose 170 basis points year over year to 12.1%.Forecast: Vacancy is expected to tick up 20 basis points to 9.3% by year-end 2026, though it would remain 10 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Rents:Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month. items.description: Press Releases Media Contacts Social Media Directory Press Kit Press Releases S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index Reports Annual Gain in August 2026 The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index posted a 2.1% annual gain for August 2026, up from a 1.9% rise in the previous month. U.S. home values fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August's 3.4% inflation ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the 2.1% home price gain. A nearly 9 percentage point gap separated August's strongest market (Chicago +6.7% YoY) and its weakest (Seattle -2.0% YoY), underscoring the strong regional divergence in home price trends. NEW YORK , Oct. 27, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P DJI) today released the August 2026 results for the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Indices. More than 27 years of history are available for the data series and can be accessed in full by going to www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/index-family/indicators/sp-Cotality-case-shiller . Cotality continues to have transaction delays from the recording office in Wayne County, the most populous county in the Detroit metro area. These delays impacted the August transaction data and, therefore, no valid August 2026 update of the Detroit S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index will be provided for the October 27, 2026, release date. There was, however, enough data to calculate a valid July 2026 update, which is provided in Tables 2 and 3. S&P DJI will continue to provide updates to the Detroit index values for the month(s) with missing sale transactions data. ANALYSIS "U.S. home prices declined in real terms for the 15th consecutive month in August 2026, though the gap narrowed as nominal home price growth strengthened," said Rebecca Kaufman, Associate Director of Commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "The S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller National Home Price Index rose 2.1% year-over-year in August, up from 1.9% in July, while consumer prices increased 3.4% (the same year over year gain as in July 2026). "Chicago led all metros for the sixth consecutive month, posting a 6.7% annual gain, followed by New York (6.2%) and Cleveland (4.3%). On the West coast, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the third consecutive month at 2.0%, followed by Las Vegas (-1.3%) and Denver (-0.8%). "Seasonality continued to weigh on headline monthly results. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively, while their seasonally adjusted counterparts rose 0.3% and 0.4%. The divergence suggests that the typical post-summer slowdown is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices. "Affordability, however, remains challenging. With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices." YEAR-OVER-YEAR The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index, covering all nine U.S. census divisions, reported a 2.1% annual gain for August. The 10-City Composite saw an annual increase of 3.6%, up from a 3.4% increase in the previous month. The 20-City Composite posted a year-over-year increase of 2.7%, up from a 2.5% rise in the previous month. Chicago reported the highest annual gain among the 20 cities with a 6.7% increase in August, followed by New York and Cleveland with annual increases of 6.2% and 4.3%, respectively. Seattle posted the lowest return in August, falling 2.0%. items.description: Apartment List National Rent Report By: Chris Salviati and Rob Warnock October 28, 2026 Headline Market Update: November 2026 Year-over-year rent growth in the U.S. flipped positive in October for the first time since mid-2023, though just barely. The national median rent currently stands at $1,384, and is now 0.1% greater than it was at this time last year. The vacancy rate is also gradually tightening, as the market transitions out of the soft conditions that have prevailed in recent years. That said, our newest market indicator tracking the concession rate, continues to show signs of softness. Key Stats National Median Rent: $1,384 per month as of October 2026. Year-Over-Year Rent Growth: Rents are up 0.1% compared to October 2025, marking the first time in over three years that year-over-year rent growth is positive. Month-Over-Month Rent Growth: Rents decreased 0.3% in October 2026 as the rental market enters its off-season; this marks the second consecutive monthly decline. Vacancy Rate: The national multifamily vacancy rate sits at 7% as of October 2026, remaining elevated compared to long-run norms, but continuing to decline after peaking earlier this year. Time on Market: Units are taking an average of 36 days to get leased after being listed, a bit longer than is typical for this time of year. Concessions Rate: 32% of multifamily properties nationally are offering concessions on new leases valued at one month of free rent or greater in October. The concessions rate remains four percentage points higher than at this time last year. Year-over-year rent growth flips positive for first time in over three years For years, the U.S. rental market has been experiencing a prolonged period of sluggishness, as a large wave of multifamily construction had been driving soft pricing and occupancy. However, we’re now at the tail end of that construction boom, and the market has been gradually moving toward more balanced conditions. This month’s data marks a significant milestone in that transition, as year-over-year rent growth flipped positive for the first time in over three years. Following a period of booming rent growth in 2021 and 2022, prices began to cool rapidly, and by June 2023, the national median rent was declining on a year-over-year basis. Full year rent growth was negative for three consecutive years, with prices nationally dipping by -0.8 percent in 2023, by -0.5 percent in 2024, and by -1.2 percent in 2026. Year-over-year rent growth bottomed out at -1.6 percent in April 2026, but over the past six months it has rebounded rapidly as healthy renter demand has filled vacant units and allowed property owners and operators to regain some pricing leverage. Despite the bounceback, rents are still essentially flat compared to one year ago, and are still declining in inflation-adjusted terms. Nonetheless, it’s a significant milestone for the rental market that year-over-year rent growth has now flipped positive. Even as year-year-over rent growth continues to rise, month-over-month rent growth remained negative in October, as the market experiences its typical off-season pricing dip. Fewer renters tend to move in the fall in winter months, and so property owners offer modest discounts to attract demand and fill vacant units at this time of year. But compared to recent years, this year’s fall cooldown has been significantly more subdued. Rents fell by just 0.3 percent in October compared to September; in October of last year, the month-over-month decline was nearly three times as sharp at -0.8 percent. In fact this month’s decline was even slightly more modest than the 2017 to 2019 average (-0.4 percent), a period when the national rental market was in a well-balanced state. In dollar terms, the national median monthly rent now stands at $1,384, up just $1 compared to October 2025. Prices peaked in mid-2022, and have since fallen from that peak by a total of 4 percent, or $58 per month. The national median rent also recently hit a notable milestone – years of modest declines have now offset the rapid price growth that preceded it such that prices are converging back to their long run trend. After oscillating between alternating hot and cool spells throughout the 2020s, the national median rent today is roughly where it would have been if rents had continued to grow at a slow and steady pace of +2.5 percent annually, the average rent growth from 2017 to 2019. This convergence has occurred just as rent growth appears set to stabilize back to something resembling that late-2010s average. Our new concessions rate indicator continues to show some softness This month, in an effort to continue providing actionable, real-time data on the rental market, the Apartment List Economics Team is adding a new dataset to our suite of market indicators: concession rates. Properties that are struggling with occupancy often employ concessions as a strategy for securing new leases. Concessions can take many forms, including discounted rents, cash back offers, gift cards, or free amenities. Such concessions are not factored into our rent estimates, and so tracking them separately provides additional nuance on market conditions. Our published concession rate represents the share of properties offering any discount whose total value is equal to one free month of rent or greater. As of October, 32 percent of all properties are offering concessions valued at one month of free rent or greater. The current concession rate is four percentage points higher than this time last year, when 28 percent of properties were offering such discounts. The concession rate has also ticked up very slightly over the past two months as we enter the off-season. Washington, D.C. – U.S. house prices rose nationwide in August, up 0.3 percent from the previous
month, according to the U.S. Federal Housing (FHFA) seasonally adjusted monthly House Price
Index (FHFA HPI®). House prices rose 2.4 percent from August 2025 to August 2026. The
previously reported 0.3 percent price increase in July was revised down to 0.2 percent.

For the nine census divisions, seasonally adjusted monthly home price changes ranged from -0.8
percent in the New England division to +2.1 percent in the East South Central division. The 12-
month changes ranged from +0.5 percent in the Mountain division to +4.4 percent in the East North
Central division.

The FHFA HPI is a comprehensive collection of publicly available house price indexes that tracks
changes in single-family home values across the United States. The data extend back to the mid-1970s
and cover all 50 states and more than 400 American cities. Drawing on information from over 100
million home sales and refinance transactions, the FHFA HPI provides detailed insights into house price
trends at the national, census division, state, metropolitan area, county, ZIP code, and census tract
levels. FHFA employs a transparent, weighted repeat-sales methodology to measure changes in home
prices using historical housing transaction data.

FHFA releases HPI data and reports quarterly and monthly. The flagship FHFA HPI uses seasonally
adjusted, purchase-only data from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Additional indexes use other data,
including refinances, mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration, and real property
records. All the indexes (including their historic values) and information about future HPI release dates
are available on FHFA’s website: https://www.fhfa.gov/HPI.

The next HPI report will be released on November 24, 2026, and will include monthly data through
September 2026 and quarterly data through the third quarter of 2026.

items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. items.title: Realpage Economy Express Episode 73
items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 73 by Arben Skivjani Posted October 19, 2026 in Insights Hotter-than-expected September inflation readings at both the consumer and wholesale level have strengthened the case for a second Fed rate hike ahead of the late October meeting. The consumer price report showed prices rose 0.6% in September, lifting the annual rate to 3.7%, the highest since May. Core inflation also picked up to 2.6%, with airfares, used cars, medical care and apparel all moving higher. According to the producer price report, wholesale prices jumped 1.3% in a single month, the biggest gain since early 2022, and were up 6.3% from a year ago. Goods prices alone rose 2.6%, the most since the series began in 2009. Minutes from the Fed's September meeting reveal that every official backed the rate hike and most expect another by year-end. The Fed's Beige Book found prices rising fast in three districts and accelerating in four. Markets now see another hike by December as very likely and put a 1-in-4 chance on two more. Retail sales data for September showed a 0.8% increase, but with prices up 0.6%, most of that gain reflects higher prices rather than more purchases. Weekly jobless claims, at 199,000, show the labor market is still holding up even as consumer sentiment sits at its lowest since May's record low. Mortgage rates have climbed to 7.5%, the highest since late 2023, according to mortgage market data, while existing home sales stayed under 4 million. For more information on the state of the U.S. Economy, including forecasts, watch all the episodes of the Economy Express series. items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 10/29/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.24% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.60% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline Further to 7.24% The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.24% as of October 29, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.32%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.17%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.60%, down from last week when it averaged 6.68%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: Weather rewrites home value
items.description: Weather is one of the oldest small talk topics there is, but in hurricane-prone Dare County, North Carolina, it stopped being small talk in 2023. That year, 13% of property insurance policies weren’t renewed, and home values fell about 10%. By 2025, price growth had turned negative. Homeowners did nothing wrong. The weather changed. ‍ For decades, historical knowledge priced environmental risk as floods came on a somewhat predictable schedule, and hurricanes followed predictable seasonal patterns. Insurers wrote policies accordingly. But Cotality's latest data analysis in the United States and Australia shows the arrangement has broken, and that relationship will only become shakier heading into 2040. Historical patterns no longer offer a reliable baseline for what's to come. The weather template is changing — it’s affecting the price of homeowner security, and home values are starting to reflect the difference. ‍ Comparing home price and insurance non-renewals: Dare County, North Carolina Data source: Cotality, 2026 Priced out of safety Miami and Naples in Florida sit among the top three U.S. cities with the most homes exposed to three natural perils simultaneously over the next 30 years. A year ago, both were migration magnets, with median prices outpacing the national average. Now, the tide has turned. Miami's market flatlined in February 2026. Naples saw price growth fall 8.3%, according to Cotality’s Home Price Index. ‍ The impact of natural disasters on real estate Data source: Cotality, 2026 California is home to a similar scenario. The state has some of the highest home prices in the U.S., which limits the buyer pool. Those who do buy a home generally take out a mortgage. That mortgage requires insurance — but getting coverage is no longer a guarantee. Wildfire risk caused many major insurers to stop writing new policies in the state where losses are mounting — Cotality research found that annual wildfire losses are projected to reach $54 million in Nevada County alone over the next 15 years. In areas like Lake County, California, the costs of environmental risk are giving carriers pause, and have pushed the insurance non-renewal rates to 7.6% in 2023. Those who can afford to still buy a home often ask for a risk discount. Environmental risk in homebuying kicks off a downward pricing trend that can depress the market over time. Already, the state has seen negative price growth in 2026. Dive deeper Comprehensive chronic climate risk assessments Between 2026 and 2040, Cotality’s Climate Risk Analytics identified current “safe” markets that will become uninsurable housing markets. Current climate risk averages ‍ Climate risk averages in 2040 Data source: Cotality, 2026 Australia is seeing a similar trend. The three towns flooded in 2022 — Lismore, Mullumbimby, Ballina — sit 5% below their pre-flood values, and buyers haven't returned. Yet, just to the north, coastal South-East Queensland, also flooded, rebounded within months and now sits 31% above pre-flood prices. Lifestyle-driven demand in that region appears to be holding the price up where it can. Where it can't, the weather-driven discount sticks. Climate risk assessment of Australian communities Data source: Cotality, 2026 ‍ "The combination of extensive damage and persistent risk of disruption in these areas of northern New South Wales isn't compensated for by the lifestyle demand seen in coastal suburbs of Queensland," said Richard Griffiths, Cotality's Head of Sustainability Solutions. Don't discount disaster: Environmental risk in homebuying Hurricanes and wildfires in California and Florida tend to get the media attention, but trouble is also present up in the middle of the country, where hail, tornadoes and storms are running up the bill one premium hike at a time. In Winkler, Texas, nearly one in four homeowners had insurance policies dropped. In Kiowa County, Oklahoma, Cotality projects $1.4 million in additional annual storm losses across just 8,800 homes by 2040. The mathematics have tipped to the point that insurance premium and deductible increases in Kiowa County now outpace yearly equity gains. Owners are paying more to protect a home that's earning less. Such rising costs are particularly landing on Gen Z . In Nebraska and Oklahoma, 9% of mortgage applicants are under 25, drawn by lower home prices, but not always seeing the full picture when insurance is factored in. A lower mortgage today can mean a larger insurance bill tomorrow, or a buyer five years out who won't pay what the current owner did. "This is a national challenge in Australia," said Griffiths. "As climate events become more frequent, the gap in how Australian communities experience and recover from disaster will only widen, further exacerbating inequality between more desirable coastal communities and rural areas." The reality is that where weather is worsening, it adds a layer of cost to markets that were already unaffordable. The pool of viable places shrinks while the pool of buyers chasing them grows. This is a structural fault line. items.title: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter
items.description: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter October 30, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private fixed investment in student dormitories rose 2.6% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $3.8 billion. This gain marked a second consecutive quarterly increase, despite continued pressures from elevated interest rates. On a year-over-year basis, investments in dorms increased 1.1%. Private fixed investment in student housing experienced a surge after the Great Recession, as college enrollment increased from 17.2 million in 2006 to 20.4 million in 2011. However, during the pandemic, private fixed investment in student housing declined drastically from $4.4 billion (SAAR) in the last quarter of 2019 to $3.1 billion in the second quarter of 2021. According to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center , college enrollment fell by 3.6% in the fall of 2020 and by 3.1% in the fall of 2021. The latest preliminary data indicated that college enrollment held steady in fall 2026 compared with the previous year. Since the pandemic, private fixed investment in dorms has rebounded alongside a gradual recovery in college enrollments. Effective in-person learning requires college students to return to campuses, boosting the student housing sector. Still, demographic trends are reshaping the outlook for student housing. The U.S. faces slower growth in the college-age population as birth rates declined following the Great Recession. Furthermore, changing perceptions towards the value of a college degree as a guaranteed pathway to job security are all contributing to an “enrollment cliff”. Despite the improvement, several major metros continued to record elevated vacancies, led by San Francisco at 26.7%, Seattle at 24.8% and Austin at 24.5%. items.title: Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike
items.description: Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike Published on October 28th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting. The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data. The committee voted 10-2 to hold rates steady today, as expected. The dissents came from Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Fed Governor Lisa Cook. The dissent from Cook was a surprise because she is generally seen as a dove, and most observers expected the second dissent to come from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan instead. Chairman Kevin Warsh was clear, however, that they are not done hiking, saying “I’m unwilling and unable to call overall financial conditions tight,” and “We haven’t achieved price stability, but we’re working on it.” An every-other-meeting hike cadence is in line with recent comments from other Fed officials who have also expressed a desire to keep hiking in the face of a stronger economy, but also a willingness to wait for data. Ultimately, the December hike will come down to the data releases between now and then. If the data comes in as expected, a hike feels all but guaranteed. Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation. He was light on details, but starting in fall 2027, the Fed will continue to have eight meetings a year. However, only seven of those will be “live” meetings where the committee will vote on rate policy and release a post-meeting statement. The remaining meeting will be used to discuss broad monetary policy strategy. And in 2028, the ratio will change further with two out of eight meetings reserved for big picture discussion. While a significant change to Fed practice, this announcement is also not so surprising given the Chairman’s desire to fundamentally question how the Fed works. That being said, should economic conditions warrant it, the Fed could always call emergency meetings to adjust rates. Chen Zhao Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics. items.title: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity?
items.description: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity? Many owners face the challenge of bringing more money into their deal. Sometimes, the cost may outweigh the benefits. Published Oct. 30, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . These days, it feels like you can find a stat to support just about anything you want. Think inflation isn’t an issue? If you watch the Sunday political shows long enough, someone probably has numbers to support that notion. On the other side, there’s probably someone who can tell you that the third-quarter U.S. real gross domestic product growth of 3.4% is a mirage. Think Brian Schottenheimer isn’t getting enough out of the Dallas Cowboys? (Spoiler alert: he isn’t, despite this week's win.) The folks at Pro Football Focus probably have something to back those claims. The same is true in multifamily. Since I started covering this sector, the number of studies, surveys and indexes that fill my inbox each day seems to have quadrupled … at least. I delete most of these research projects or studies because much of this “research” is sent under the guise of pitching products. However, I do look at certain reports and even seek others out. As more loans face issues in the apartment industry, I recently went to CRED iQ’s website to get an idea of the size of the maturity wall. There I found something that caught my eye — an article saying nearly 33% of maturing apartment debt needs a cash infusion to refinance. At first blush, that number felt, well, kind of low, given everything that I’ve been reading about maturity walls and refinance risk. Reading further on the CRED iQ website, I learned that the firm resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028. Of that $136 billion in debt, 23% of the loans and 31% of the balance can’t refinance without an equity infusion of roughly $6.8 billion. The good news for apartment owners is that money is available to fill that gap. The bad news: It’s getting more expensive. Earlier this year, Maximiliane Leachman, vice chair of CBRE’s debt and structured finance group, told me refinancing is becoming harder for some borrowers. At one point, these lenders may have wanted 1% to 3% of the loan balance for an extension. Now, many could be looking for 10%. “We’re all waiting for the shoe to drop at the end of this year as those borrowers come back for the second time to that debt fund for another modification,” Leachman said. “It will be interesting to see how many of those go back.” But costs aren’t the only issues owners must weigh when deciding whether to bring additional capital into their deals. In a recent conversation, Michael Lynd, CEO of Kairoi Residential, raised another concern: whether refinancing is worth the cost to existing equity holders. “The question that I have when I look at a lot of these refinances is the cost of that refinance is not great for your existing equity,” Lynd said. “If rent growth doesn’t show up in that first six to nine months or a year, then you have a chance of further impairing the equity value that isn't in place.” Lynd thinks a lot of groups are making decisions that might not be in their investors’ best interests by holding on to properties rather than selling them because they don’t want a negative trade on their record. Alternatively, they may want to delay a sale to raise additional capital. “I see it happening all over the place,” Lynd said. “You can get a loan, but should you take that loan? Is that the best risk-adjusted decision for your equity?” If the answer is no and if the market doesn’t snap back, those firms might be doing their investors a disservice. Still, some owners may find data showing refinancing is the best option. And it could be. But just because you can find the data to say something doesn’t make it so. items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The Federal Open Market Committee decided to keep the benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75% and 4% at the conclusion of its October meeting. The central bank’s benchmark rate influences a wide range of consumer borrowing and savings costs. As long as the Fed keeps rates elevated, consumers are unlikely to see much relief from the high prices and higher borrowing costs that continue to weigh on household budgets. watch now VIDEO 5:49 05:49 Barclays' Giannoni sees Fed hiking in Dec and Jan as inflation pressures persist Squawk Box Asia The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, even as rising energy costs threaten to keep inflation elevated and further strain already-tight household budgets. Higher energy prices stemming from the Iran war may prove stickier than expected, but the central bank's decision to hold rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess the economic fallout. The dynamic could also lead Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee to consider raising rates at their December meeting in order to bring inflation down to the Fed's 2% target. For now, however, persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs are compounding affordability challenges for many households, economists say. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said in a post on Oct. 12 that the war has cost the average American household about $2,000 so far, mostly due to higher energy costs, in addition to heightened interest rate costs. "High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto," Zandi told CNBC. "Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders." How the Fed impacts your money The Federal Reserve's decision to keep rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline, means consumers are unlikely to see much relief from high borrowing costs anytime soon. The Fed influences the federal funds rate, an interest rate benchmark that sets what banks charge each other for overnight lending. That rate ripples throughout the economy, influencing both consumer borrowing costs and returns on savings. Short-term consumer lending rates, such as credit cards, closely track the prime rate, which typically moves in tandem with the Fed's benchmark and is generally about 3 percentage points higher. Longer-term rates, like those on 30-year mortgages, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and the economic outlook. Because most cards have variable rates, borrowers typically see changes in the federal funds rate passed on within one to two billing cycles. But even as the Fed's benchmark rate has largely held steady — except for September's 25-basis-point increase — the average credit card interest rate has been trending higher amid concerns of rising delinquencies in the face of stubborn inflation, according to LendingTree. "Credit card rates have risen for three straight months and are now at their highest levels since December 2025," said Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief consumer finance analyst. "Rates are highly likely to rise in the next few months, too, as card issuers implement the Fed's September hike," he added. A sign is posted in front of a home for sale in Los Angeles, California, on Sept. 3, 2026. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Unlike credit cards and other variable-rate loans, 15- and 30-year fixed mortgage rates don't move in lockstep with the Fed's benchmark rate. Instead, they generally track long-term Treasury yields , which have recently climbed amid concerns that ongoing U.S.-Iran tensions and higher energy costs could keep inflation elevated. As a result, 30-year fixed mortgage rates have remained above 7% for more than a month, according to Mortgage News Daily . "There is no single switch that will bring mortgage rates meaningfully lower," said Jeff DerGurahian, LoanDepot's chief investment officer and head economist. "We likely need several factors to fall into place, including cooler oil prices, softer consumer spending and a steady run of inflation reports showing progress toward the Fed's 2% target." Meanwhile, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that aims to reduce some mortgage costs as rising interest rates and inflation make homeownership less affordable .
