items.title: For Fed, politics impossible to avoid in pre-midterm FOMC
items.description: Monetary policy For Fed, politics impossible to avoid in pre-midterm FOMC By Kyle Campbell CloseText About Kyle twitter ByKyleCampbell Published October 28, 2026, 6:00 a.m. EDT | Updated October 28, 2026, 3:23 p.m. EDT 7 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman. Federal Reserve Board Processing Content Key insight: The midterm elections are likely shaping market expectations about the Federal Open Market Committee's policy more than the decision itself. But the political implications are still consequential. Expert quote: "The Fed stresses very much its own independence and its political independence. They wouldn't want to be seen, for instance, raising rates and hurting the administration, the economy in general." — Dan North, senior economist for Allianz Trade Americas The Federal Open Market Committee is broadly expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite signs that inflation is worsening. More than 90% of federal funds futures contracts are pricing in no change to the benchmark rate after Wednesday's meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool, despite nearly 84% of the market anticipating at least one 25 basis point increase before the end of the year. There are several dynamics driving this sentiment. Some economists question the effectiveness of the Fed's policy tools in the current environment. Others are simply following the latest guidance from FOMC participants — outdated as it might be. Then there's the politics of it all. Because of next week's midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years, some analysts believe the Fed will be reluctant to deliver a surprise hike, lest it be seen as putting its thumb on the scale of public sentiment. "We've got the midterms coming up next week, so that is a little bit of a delicate situation," said Dan North, senior economist for Allianz Trade Americas. "I think the Fed will take the position of doing nothing, because if they were to raise rates, that would raise questions about political favor, somehow, on the Federal Reserve. They want to avoid that." President Donald Trump — who stands to lose his governing majority and face myriad congressional investigations into his administration should Democrats take one or both of the houses — is always ready to criticize the central bank for what he sees as partisan policy actions. But North said the issue is not Trump-specific. He would expect the Fed to steer clear of the political fray under any administration. Not because a single rate hike would change the economic outlook dramatically in one week — such changes take months to take effect — but because of the optics. "The Fed stresses very much its own independence and its political independence," North said. "They wouldn't want to be seen, for instance, raising rates and hurting the administration, the economy in general." The historical record on FOMC activity ahead of midterm elections is thin and the results are mixed. Since 1954, the committee has convened in October or early November ahead of a midterm election 11 times, according to data on committee votes maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Those meetings have resulted in three rate hikes, four rate decreases and four instances of no change. For all federal elections — including presidential cycles as well as midterms — the results are similar: the FOMC dropped rates 10 times, raised them six and held them steady nine. There were also 10 election cycles in which the Fed did not vote immediately before ballots were cast but instead, met in late September and again shortly after the election. More recently, rate increases directly before federal elections have become increasingly rare. The committee has approved just one pre-election hike since 1980: a 75 basis point increase directly before the last set of midterms in 2022. That jumbo rate hike was the fourth consecutive three-quarter-point increase by the FOMC, its sixth raise in as many meetings and part of an overall policy tightening campaign that saw the federal funds rate increase more than 5 percentage points in a single year. This is emblematic of other pre-election rate increases. Such moves have tended to be part of hiking cycles that span several consecutive meetings. Read more: As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS? Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated In theory, the Fed could be at the beginning of such a cycle. The FOMC raised rates in September, most committee members expected to raise at least once more this year and the Fed's primary concern at the moment — persistently high inflation — appears to be trending in the wrong direction . The consumer price index was up 3.7% year over year in September, with input prices rising even more sharply . "All in all, economic data suggest that there is no good reason for the Fed to delay tightening monetary policy," said Jerry Tempelman, former senior analyst at the New York Fed and current vice president of economic and fixed income research at Mutual of America Capital Management. But recent commentary from Fed officials suggests the current tightening campaign might move in fits and starts. In a speech earlier this month, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said he supported the hike last month as a way of shoring up the Fed's credibility, rather than an outright effort to crush inflation. "This was an important step to ensure longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored and to validate the public's confidence that we will achieve our 2% inflation objective in a timely manner," Jefferson said. There is some evidence that market confidence has been restored. Yields for 10- and 30-year Treasuries have declined about 30 basis points

items.title: UK Budget Risks Deterring Sovereign Wealth Funds From Real Estate
items.description: The budget is out, and the property industry has concerns. UK Chancellor John Healey avoided a bond-market shock with his “breathing space” budget , and the immediate financial-market reaction was reassuring. Gilt yields did not spike, avoiding an outcome that could have pushed financing costs up even further. However, investors were left waiting for measures capable of bringing borrowing costs down and stimulating new development. The budget also delivered limited progress on development viability, while business rates measures offered some relief to high street occupiers without delivering the structural reform sought by many property owners. But new proposed tax rules for sovereign investors, which threaten to make the UK less attractive to global property capital, caused a sharp intake of breath. Flickr/House of Commons Chancellor John Healey succeeded in placating bond markets, but the property sector raised concerns over sovereign taxes. The government has launched a consultation over its proposal to replace the largely noncodified sovereign immunity from direct taxation with a statutory regime from 1 January 2029. Certain UK property income and capital gains would become taxable, although the reforms include bespoke access to the real estate investment trust regime, with a 15% tax rate on qualifying property income distributions. State-operated overseas pension funds and certain investment management activities would remain exempt. The government claimed the reforms would improve transparency and provide greater certainty for sovereign investors, but many in the property industry worry it could weaken the UK's appeal to investors. “It’s a really unhelpful change,” Real Estate:UK Assistant Director of Finance Rachel Kelly said. She said the proposal introduces additional costs for a significant source of real estate investment while development viability is already under severe pressure. Sovereign wealth funds invested £6.2B in UK property from 2021 to 2024, according to a March report from BPF and CoStar . Although the proposed REIT arrangements and transitional provisions offer some flexibility, the new 15% rate would be a significant increase for qualifying sovereign investors accustomed to paying no tax. It also adds an onerous process. “In addition to the actual additional cost now of investing in the UK for those investors, there will be huge complexity in terms of having to restructure their investments, and there will be a lot of work for some to change how they're structured,” Kelly said. The implications extend beyond the funds themselves. Sovereign wealth funds frequently invest alongside other capital providers, meaning changes to their investment structures could affect co-investors and joint ventures too, Moorfield CEO Charles Ferguson-Davie said. He said the reforms risk sending the wrong signal. “There aren’t that many groups that will deploy over £500M, over a billion,” Ferguson-Davie said. “If they’re going to be less active as a result of having to pay tax, who’s going to step in and invest that money instead?” CBRE Investment Management is looking to understand the rules in more detail during the consultation, Director Alex Lund said. But he expressed optimism that the policy won’t decimate investment. “For any market looking to attract overseas capital ... taxes and the need for a level playing field for domestic and international investors are very important,” he said. “But many investors are already in the UK, which is a large, deep and transparent market, so we would remain positive while looking at the consultation carefully.” Ferguson-Davie said the wider economic benefits of attracting large-scale investment should be part of the government's calculations, rather than focusing solely on the tax revenue generated. He said the string of regulatory or tax burdens added to the private rental sector over the last few budgets show the danger in the government’s thinking. “You can understand the political motivation, but it has already led to a lot of sales and exits from the market,” Ferguson-Davie said. “I'm not sure it's all necessarily ending up benefiting the renter.” Instead, supply and development have both fallen, and that pushes rents up. He said the new budget will encourage the sale of buy-to-lets, which could benefit the institutional build-to-rent sector — but it doesn’t actually solve any problems. “What the BTR community needs, indeed the housing sector needs, is more incentives to help bring down the cost of development,” he said. “If we're going to have a meaningful change in terms of new houses delivered for sale and for rent, we need the regulatory and tax burden reduced, because otherwise it's just going to get worse.” BTR construction starts have fallen 63% in the last year, with only 4,696 groundbreakings in September, versus 12,674 the year prior, according to Savills data for RE:UK . “Investors needed more than a pause in policy changes,” Kelly said. The budget's business rates package provided more immediate support for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. However, Kelly said the chancellor again failed to deliver meaningful long-term reform. items.title: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers – Insurance Business
items.description: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers A White House plan to pull private mortgage insurance off loans sooner, and to let refinancing borrowers skip the lender's title policy, affects two insurance lines that say they already help keep costs down PROPERTY By Stephen Owens Oct 25, 2026 Share Mortgage insurers and title underwriters are the latest targets of the White House's pre-election push on housing costs. President Donald Trump on Oct. 22 signed an executive order, Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People , that leans on the Federal Housing Finance Agency to squeeze costs out of the mortgage process. Two of its four main provisions deal with insurance: a pilot to cancel mortgage insurance premiums ahead of schedule, and a permanent version of FHFA's experiment letting some refinances skip the traditional lender's title policy, according to the White House fact sheet . The rest of the order sets up a federal task force on factory-built housing and tells the Agriculture and Veterans Affairs departments to cut rates on their direct home loans. FHFA Director Bill Pulte called it "the greatest Housing Executive Order in History" on X. The fact sheet, however, sets no equity thresholds, no start dates and no estimate of how many loans would qualify, so mortgage insurers, title underwriters and agents can't yet tell how much business is at stake. Read next: Why home insurance prices are quietly becoming a 2026 midterm flashpoint Mortgage insurers say cancellation rules already exist The mortgage insurance piece would have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac use automated valuation models to recheck home values on loans they own from time to time, then drop the coverage once a borrower appears to have built enough equity, according to Mortgage Professional America's breakdown of the order . Servicers would have to tell borrowers when cancellation might be possible. The pilot covers only loans originated after it launches. Borrowers already paying premiums would not benefit directly. Mortgage insurers point out that borrowers already have cancellation rights. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, borrower-paid coverage on a conventional loan must end automatically once the balance hits 78% of the home's original value, and borrowers can ask to cancel at 80%, with some able to qualify on the strength of home price gains if conditions are met, according to U.S. Mortgage Insurers (USMI) , the trade group whose members include Enact, Essent, MGIC, National MI and Radian. USMI President Seth Appleton welcomed the focus on costs and said the industry was already lowering them. "Private MI is designed to be temporary, and the system already works much the way the order envisions, because when MI is cancelled, a borrower's monthly payment goes down," he said in the group's statement. USMI's statement describes the order as telling FHFA to consider a pilot, not to launch one. The group says premium rates have fallen 25% since 2017, that more than 800,000 buyers used private coverage in 2025, two-thirds of them first-timers, and that its members insure more than $1.6 trillion in mortgages. Insurers have paid over $62 billion in claims since 2008 that would otherwise have hit the government-sponsored enterprises, lenders and investors, USMI said. The pilot could also affect pricing. Mortgage insurance is priced on how long an insurer expects to keep collecting premiums. Some industry voices warned that a program clipping off late-life, low-risk loans could push insurers to build that lost income into pricing on new business, MPA reported . The order comes during a strong year for mortgage insurers. New insurance written across the six active private insurers (Arch, Enact, Essent, MGIC, NMI and Radian) hit a multi-year high in the second quarter of 2026, with strong credit performance, according to Milliman's quarterly market update . Read next : Old Republic prevails as Massachusetts court rejects title coverage expansion Title waiver pilot would become permanent For title underwriters, the order expands a program their trade group has opposed since 2024. The title acceptance pilot dates to March 2024, when the Biden-era FHFA approved waiving the lender's title policy, or an attorney opinion letter, on certain low-risk refinances where there is confidence the property is free of prior liens, according to a statement from then-Director Sandra Thompson . Fannie Mae launched it in November 2024 with Doma Title Insurance and added Westcor Land Title Insurance Co. in July 2025. Pulte said in June that Fannie would grow it. The order would make the program permanent and broaden it. The order directs FHFA to lift the current 80% loan-to-value cap on eligibility, bring in more title-assessment providers and scrap the geographic limits, according to MPA's reading of the text. It also calls for waiving appraisals and income re-verification on limited cash-out refinances that cut a borrower's monthly payment. The American Land Title Association responded the same day, warning that any cost-cutting push must keep protections for homeowners and their property rights in place rather than shift risk to consumers and taxpayers. In 2024, ALTA called the original pilot a political gesture that offered a false promise of savings. Analysts expect a limited effect for now. Analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods wrote in an Oct. 21 note that refinances account for only about 7% of title premiums, so the earnings hit should be modest while the program stays refi-only. They said the risk would be greater if the waiver ever reached purchase loans, where there is no scalable substitute for a title policy. Refinance volume is low with 30-year rates above 7%, but a rate drop would quickly enlarge the pool of loans eligible for a waiver, and the order would also remove the program's geographic limits. items.title: Case-Shiller: Phoenix home-price growth increases in August
items.description: Case-Shiller: Phoenix home-price growth increases in August by John Yellig October 27, 2026 The pace of home-price growth across the United States continued to accelerate in August despite varying widely between markets. No. 1 Chicago saw prices jump, while lowest-ranked Seattle saw a decline. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index rose 2.1% year over year in August, up from a 1.9% gain in July. Month over month, the index slipped 0.02%. S&P Dow Jones noted that home values actually fell in real terms for the 15th month in a row, as August's 3.4% inflation erased the 2.1% gain in prices. “U.S. home prices declined in real terms for the 15th consecutive month in August 2026, though the gap narrowed as nominal home price growth strengthened,” said Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "Affordability, however, remains challenging. With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices.” In Phoenix, home prices inched 0.42% higher year over year and slipped 0.53% month over month in August. items.title: A path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table
items.description: Housing demand has stabilized over the last two weeks as rates have fallen a tad, and we can finally see a clear path back to sub-7% mortgage rates . We survived the crazy month of October, when the 10-year had the potential to close above 5.35%, which would have created a backdrop of bond-escalation selling, sending mortgage rates above 8%. That didn’t happen, of course, as the 10-year yield held that key line! Not only has the 10-year yield now gone below 5% — with mortgage rates closer to 7% than 8% today — but what this month has shown us is that there’s a clear path for sub-7% mortgage rates. Just the move in the last two weeks has stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, so let’s take a look on this Halloween on what needs to happen to get rates lower. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week was Fed week, and even Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said tighter policy has created financial pain for some AI companies. The Federal Reserve has been talking more and more about AI being very inflationary for many weeks now, so naturally, when AI companies are having debt-financing issues, and some are missing on their numbers, the 10-year yield has gone lower even with elevated oil prices and economic data staying firm. However, imagine for a minute that the Iran conflict was over: oil would be trading between $67 and $82. Imagine that the trade war 2.0 doesn’t get worse and you have an AI slowdown; there’s your trinity for lower mortgage rates. Nothing too drastic, but definitely sub-7%, and we’ve all seen what mortgage demand can do when rates drop below 6.64%. So there’s a pathway to 7%, but there’s also a pathway for rates to stay above 7% if the AI story rebounds, the conflict doesn’t end, and the trade war continues. This, of course, would need the economic data to stay very positive, as it has recently. Since Sept. 10, a clear head-and-shoulders pattern has formed in the 10-year yield so what I said above can break that lower and get us sub-7% rates. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multi-year lows. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%, since mortgage rates would already be over 8% now if this were not the case. Not only that, it would have been impossible to get mortgage rates near 7% again without a much bigger move lower with the 10-year yield. That said, when the 10-year yield moves lower at times, spreads can widen after a big move up because their job is to compress volatility. Now, this does wear off over time, and we can head lower again. What you don’t want to see is the Fed suddenly changing course and starting a massive rate-hike cycle, or a credit event like the Silicon Valley Bank crisis. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads were flat at 2.23% from week to week. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level: If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.15% today, not 7.27%. If we had the worst levels of 2024, mortgage rates would be 7.77% today. If we had the worst levels of 2025, mortgage rates would be 7.58% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last two weeks: lower rates even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending home sales are still higher than two weeks ago. That is all we should take from this move, and we will see how rates affect the data going forward. Rule of thumb for the last three years and 10 months: housing demand typically grows when rates are under 6.64% and heading toward 6%, and doesn’t show growth when rates are over 6.64% and heading above 7%. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 52,050 2025: 55,214 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. I expected some week-to-week growth last week, as our tracker showed growth too; we did have a 4% week-to-week gain, but it's still down significantly year over year. When rates were closer to 6%, every week except one showed year-over-year growth. However, higher mortgage rates and weaker mortgage demand create more inventory, and the year-over-year comps are much easier now than early in the year. items.title: National Home Value Growth Accelerates Yet Continues To Trail Inflation
items.description: Trends Follow Us On Google National Home Value Growth Accelerates Yet Continues To Trail Inflation By Snejana Farberov October 27, 2026 SeanPavonePhoto/Adobe Stock National home values posted modest gains in August, picking up speed from July, though price growth still failed to keep pace with inflation. The value of single-family homes as measured by repeat transactions rose 2.1% year over year in August, up from a 1.9% annual increase the month before, according to data from the S P Cotality Case-Shiller Index released Tuesday. The more robust growth came even as the median existing-home sales price slowed to a 1.6% annual gain in August. However, while nominal home values accelerated nationally, they fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August's 3.4% inflation rate ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the home value gain. Across the 20 cities tracked by the index, Chicago once again took pole position, leading the U.S. for the sixth consecutive month with a 6.7% annual gain, down slightly from July. New York followed with a year-over-year increase of 6.2%. Cleveland took bronze, registering a gain of 4.3%. "Seasonality continued to weigh on headline monthly results," says Rebecca Kaufman , associate director of commodities at S P Dow Jones Indices. "On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively, while their seasonally adjusted counterparts rose 0.3% and 0.4%. The divergence suggests that the typical post-summer slowdown is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices." Loading... However, Kaufman concedes that affordability remains a challenge. Referring to August data before mortgage rates crossed the 7% threshold, she notes: "With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices." The latest Case-Shiller report highlights a persistent regional divergence in home prices. Seattle posted the nation's steepest annual decline for the third month in a row, slipping 1.6%, followed by Las Vegas (-1.3%), and Denver (-0.8%). "The years-long East-West divide persists, with six out of the eight Eastern metropolitan markets recording greater year-over-year changes in July versus June, compared with just two of the eight Western metropolitan markets," says Kaufman. As in June and July, a gap of nearly 9 percentage points separated the strongest housing market, Chicago, which was bolstered by tight resale supply and limited new construction, from the weakest, Seattle. Loading... What this means for homebuyers Looking ahead, Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith reminds that the rate backdrop has become considerably more challenging since the end of August. The 30-year fixed rate climbed to 7.40% in mid-October, the highest level of the year, before easing to 7.32% as of Oct. 22 , after the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate on Sept. 16 and September Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose to 3.7%. Pending home sales plunged 7.3% in September to the lowest reading on record and were down 11.3% from a year ago, with declines in all four regions. "With inventory at its highest level since 2019 and rates above 7%, buyers have more homes to choose from but less power to pay for them," says Smith. The Case-Shiller Index reports on a two-month delay and reflects a three-month moving average of home sales prices. Homes usually go under contract a month or two before they close, so the August report primarily reflects purchase decisions made in late spring and early summer. Although the Index's price data is delayed by several months, it is considered one of the best available measures of changing home values, because it is based on repeat transactions on the same properties. Vacancy increased 10 bps QOQ to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 psf in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. Supply Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 million square feet (msf) underway. Construction commenced on nearly 63,000 square feet (sf) of new retail space during the quarter. Meanwhile, deliveries totaled 78,000 sf, bringing year-to-date (YTD) deliveries to 158,000 sf. This represented a 64.6% year-over-year (YOY) decrease from the 447,000 sf delivered during the same period in 2025. Vacancy increased 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Despite the slight increase, Miami-Dade County’s retail market continued to demonstrate tight conditions, with vacancy remaining the lowest among Florida markets, below Fort Lauderdale at 4.2%, Orlando at 3.9% and Tampa at 3.8%. Demand Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. The market recorded negative 81,000 sf of net absorption during the quarter, bringing the YTD total to negative 129,000 sf. Although occupancy losses have persisted in six of the past seven quarters, quarterly performance improved considerably from negative 230,000 sf in the third quarter of 2025. At the submarket level, Kendall and Miami Airport led occupancy gains, recording 97,000 sf and nearly 51,000 sf of positive absorption, respectively. These gains were offset by losses in Coral Gables (negative 41,000 sf) and Northeast Dade (negative 35,000 sf). By property type, malls posted the strongest performance, with occupancy gains of just under 12,000 sf, while general retail recorded the largest decline at negative 62,000 sf. Overall, leasing activity and occupancy trends remained mixed across the county, with gains in select submarkets and property types offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Looking ahead, the construction pipeline may provide additional opportunities for retailers as new space enters the market, although future occupancy gains will depend on demand keeping pace with new supply. Pricing Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 per square foot (psf) in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Among the county’s retail submarkets, Miami Beach commanded the highest average asking rent at $97.85 psf, while Miami recorded the lowest at $31.92 psf. Compared YOY, average asking rents increased in 16 submarkets and declined in three. Outlying Miami-Dade County recorded the largest YOY increase, with rents rising 4.1% from $40.97 psf to $42.65 psf. In contrast, Brickell asking rents declined 2.4% YOY to $84.96 psf. Retail Sales Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. This brought YTD transaction volume to $1.2 billion across 2.0 msf. YTD transaction volume declined 25.5% YOY and was 6.6% below the five-year average. Miami Airport led all submarkets with $265.8 million in sales. Notable transactions included the $72.0 million sale of Airpark Plaza, located at 5715 NW Seventh Street in the Miami Airport submarket. By property type, strip malls recorded the highest average sale price at $815 psf during the quarter. Pricing remained elevated, with Miami averaging $450 psf, well above the U.S. average of $246 psf, underscoring the market’s continued premium positioning. Miami-Dade County’s retail capitalization rates ranged from 4.9% to 7.2%, averaging 5.8%. This was below the national average of 7.4%, indicating that local retail properties continued to trade at lower yields than the national average. items.title: The housing market gets a positive Fed day for a change
items.description: On Wednesday we got an October surprise: the Fed day was eerily calm, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh looking comfortable on stage and offering a slightly dovish take on the future — if a few things improve. I believe the Fed wants to take back all the interest rate cuts from last year, and then they can assess what is happening in the economy. Of course, the Iran conflict and Trade War 2.0 have complicated their job, but today, given that markets were at one point pricing in five to six rate hikes, was a positive day. Last I checked, the 10-year was at 5.02%, down after Google reported a bad quarter. The Fed's press statement was short and simple, but two things caught my attention. 1. The economy is strong vs. solid First, the Fed chose to use the word "strong" instead of "solid" on purpose to signal it won’t cut rates and will continue reversing last year's interest rate cuts while inflation stays above target. “ Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Warsh said jobless claims data remain low and that the Fed fully intends to bring inflation back to the 2% target, no compromise. He also said the Fed will hold one fewer voting meeting in 2027 and two fewer meetings in 2028; this approach might leave the Fed open to more 50-basis-point cuts or hikes. However, that is another story for another time. 2. Warsh liked the market drama against AI I got a strong sense that Warsh liked the market getting more restrictive and that we even saw some AI companies shed some blood recently. My theme in the HousingWire Daily podcast lately borrows from The Predator movie: the AI god king can bleed — and that it means you can kill it. I think Warsh was implying no company is invincible, and that if the market gets more restrictive, things can change, as they recently did. He also talked about how the 10-year yield rolled over even though oil prices have been elevated this month. I believe the 10-year yield rollover is more market-driven, as the 10-year was pricing in more rate hikes than the Fed was targeting at the time. The term premium on the 10-year yield was elevated as it headed to the October high. If the 10-year had closed over the key level of 5.35%, bond yields had the potential to rise much higher, faster, as the markets would be pricing in a much more aggressive Fed rate hike cycle, but, smartly, they chose not to go that route. Warsh seems to enjoy that everyone is taking the Fed seriously and that the markets have already done a lot of the work for them. This reaffirms my assumption that all they want to do is take back the rate cuts from last year and then reassess what is going on. One side note was that Fed Governor Lisa Cook — who is usually a dove — voted to raise rates, which I 100% believe was a trolling tactic on her part since Trump still wants to fire her . All in all, it wasn’t a bad day; the 10-year yield is above 5% still today, but considering the market was trying to price in five to six rate hikes, and there hasn’t been any end to the conflict or the trade war, I consider this a victory for the month of October. For housing, the worst-case scenario has been averted and we bought some time, giving space for the conflict to end and the trade war to cool off a bit. What I am hoping for is that we get some more clarity on both of those two items, and then the Fed can make the rate hike cycle just a few rate hikes, and then we'll take it from there. items.title: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained
items.description: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 21, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Don't expect single-family construction to accelerate anytime soon. Consumer and builder confidence has weakened, while mortgage rates, financing costs, construction expenses, labor costs and regulatory hurdles continue to weigh on development activity. At the same time, ongoing affordability concerns and elevated home prices are limiting housing demand. Single-family housing starts surged above 1.3 million units on a seasonally adjusted basis during the post-pandemic period of exceptionally low mortgage rates. As borrowing costs climbed and mortgage rates moved above 7%, housing starts fell to roughly 800,000 units by late 2022. Annualized starts activity later recovered to more than one million units before gradually easing back toward 900,000 units in 2026. With mortgage rates averaging roughly 7.4% in October, pressure on the single-family sector is likely to persist. September’s seasonally adjusted rate for single-family starts was 859,000 units, down 4.6% from August’s revised rate but up 2.6% from one year ago. Annualized single-family permits fell 4% from August and 4.8% from last September to a 3.5-year low of 845,000 units. The number of single-family homes currently under construction was unchanged month-to-month at 587,000 units, but that annualized rate was down 2.8% from last September. Single-family completions dipped 2.4% for the month but fell 11% from one year ago to 840,000 units, while units authorized, but not started jumped 6.3% from last year to 151,000 units, the same rate as last month. Meanwhile, multifamily development faces similar headwinds with the seasonally adjusted starts rate at 349,000 units, down 7.2% from August and 25.9% from last year. Annualized multifamily permitting increased 5.9% for the month and 1% for the year to 503,000 units. Reflecting the volatility of the seasonally adjusted data series, the unadjusted annual starts and permits totals for multifamily were both up close to 7% from last September. Like the single-family series, the annualized rate of multifamily units under construction was unchanged for the month at 677,000 units, however, that was down 3.1% for the year. Authorized multifamily units that were not started were also unchanged for the month at 123,000 units but were up 13.9% for the year. Multifamily completions rose 14.9% from August to 339,000 units but were down 20.4% for the year. Compared to one year ago, the annual rate for multifamily permitting increased in two of the four regions, with moderate improvement in the Northeast (up 8.5% to 83,000 units) and solid growth in the Midwest (up 32.8% to 79,000 units). The West region saw the deepest decrease of 17% in annual multifamily permitting to 100,000 units in September, followed by a very modest 0.2% decrease in the South to 241,000 units. Compared to the previous month, permitting was down in the West and up in the remaining regions. Annualized multifamily starts decreased sharply in three regions: the West (down 56.7% to 48,000 units), the Midwest (down 54.4% to 35,000 units) and the Northeast (down 43.5% to 62,000 units). The South region’s multifamily starts increased 16.8% to 205,000 units. Compared to August’s seasonally adjusted annual rate, starts were up strongly in the South and down in the remaining regions. items.title: New Home Sales Slip Slightly in September
items.description: New Home Sales Slip Slightly in September By Joel Berner Oct 27, 2026 September 2026 New-Home Sales What happened this month New home sales retreated a bit from August’s performance (down 0.6% month over month) and came in behind last year’s level (down 5.3% year over year). Sales activity in the new home segment has been muted so far through 2026, running 2.9% below 2025 year to date. Buyers are reluctant in this environment of elevated mortgage rates, and builders are having to offer lower prices and buyer incentives to entice them. The median sale price in September for new homes was $400,400, 3.9% lower than in September of 2025 and once again lower than the median existing home sale price from the same month. The Northeast rebounded in new home sales after a weak August, coming in at 28.0% higher than last month and 10.3% higher than last year. The other regions all posted year-over-year losses. The West had its best month since April, including a 21.4% month-over-month improvement, but still fell 17.4% short on a year over year basis. New home sales in the Midwest fell 7.3% month over month and 8.2% year over year, while in the South they dropped 6.6% from August and 0.7% from last September. Data from the Northeast, by far the smallest region for both new construction and new home sales activity, is quite noisy, so the improvement there should be considered with some caution. Overall, the regional splits point to a new home sales slowdown that is geographically widespread. Inventory growth has slowed The number of new homes for sale fell 1.0% month over month and 2.3% year over year to 476,000, its lowest reading since September 2024. Builders are pulling back on single-family home completions, so even though fewer new homes are being sold, the number of new homes on the market is contracting. This is reflected in the months of supply figure, which fell to 8.4 this month from 8.5 last month and closer to 9 for much of 2026 so far. Builders are wary of constructing homes they will not be able to sell quickly, which is further evidenced by the stage of construction of the new homes on the market. The number of new homes for sale that have not yet been started, 115,000 of them, is the highest in data history. Meanwhile, the number of new homes under construction or completed is falling. What does this mean for buyers and builders? The new home market is still firmly in buyers’ market territory. Builders, much like existing home sellers, are being forced to compete for the attention of a dwindling pool of buyers. Unlike existing home sellers, though, builders can’t afford to keep their inventory off the market until conditions improve. They can and are slowing down on the delivery of new homes, but there are still 111,000 completed homes for sale across the country for which builders are eagerly searching for buyers. Home shoppers should consider new construction not only because of the competitive prices and incentives offered by builders, but also because of the lower total cost of ownership that newly-built homes offer over the long run.

items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. Washington, DC’s multifamily permitting was spread diversely around that metro’s area. items.title: Cooling Jobs and a Firmer Rent Outlook for 2027
items.description: Cooling Jobs and a Firmer Rent Outlook for 2027 by Arben Skivjani Posted October 12, 2026 in Market Research The energy shock that rattled the spring did less damage to growth than the early numbers suggested. GDP for 2nd quarter was revised up to 2.2% annualized in the Bureau of Economic Analysis' third estimate, well above the 1.5% first reported, with consumer spending, investment and exports adding to growth while higher imports took some back. Growth in1st quarter was also revised higher, to 2.5%. The Federal Reserve's own September projections moved the same way, with 2026 growth now seen at 2.3%. Hiring lost steam as the summer went on. July turned out to be a loss of 10,000 jobs after revisions, August added 133,000 positions and September managed just 29,000 additions, which works out to 152,000 jobs for the quarter, or about 51,000 per month. The unemployment rate and participation ticked up to 61.8% from 61.5% in June. Pay is cooling along with hiring. Average hourly earnings were up 3% year-over-year, compared with 3.5% at midyear. Prices are still running hot enough to keep the Fed on the offensive. Headline PCE was up 3.4% from a year earlier in August, still a long way from the 2% target, while core PCE, which leaves out food and energy, was calmer at 3%. In September the Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to lift the federal funds rate by one quarter point to 3.75% to 4%, aiming to bring inflation back to 2% sooner. The median projection now puts the rate near 4.1% by year-end, which implies one more increase, with PCE inflation expected to ease to 2.3% in 2027. In our latest forecast, rents find firmer footing over the coming year. Effective rents are projected to rise about 2.4% nationally from 4th quarter 2026 to 3rd quarter 2027, and more markets are joining the leaders, with nine of the top 50, or 18%, in the 3% range. San Francisco and Milwaukee lead at 3.8%, followed by Phoenix at 3.7%, and Miami, Cincinnati, Oakland, Los Angeles, Denver and San Diego all come in at 3.1% or better. Most markets, some 64%, fall between 2% and 2.9% growth, including Dallas, Austin, Chicago, Boston and Seattle. Seven markets land in the 1% range, among them New York, Washington, DC, Fort Worth and Atlanta. Only Houston (0.5%) and San Antonio (0.8%) fall below 1% as they work through recent supply. No market in the top 50 is projected to see rent decline. New supply keeps coming. We project roughly 320,000 apartments will be delivered over the next four quarters, about 85% of those units in the top 50 markets. Dallas sits at the head of the line with just over 20,000 units, trailed by New York and Newark at roughly 17,000 to 17,500 units, while Phoenix, Houston and Charlotte each add about 13,000 to 13,500 units. At the other end, Memphis, Virginia Beach, Cleveland and Oakland will each see fewer than 800 new units, with Pittsburgh and San Francisco not far behind at roughly 1,000 to 1,100 units. items.title: Abundance of Single-Family Homes in Houston May Dilute Multifamily Demand
items.description: Abundance of Single-Family Homes in Houston May Dilute Multifamily Demand by Carl Whitaker Posted October 13, 2026 in Insights Houston might be the ficklest market in the country and has been a source of disappointment for owner/operators for what feels like forever now. The metro just can't seem to sustain stretches of consistently robust demand, but that's yet to be a consistent deterrent of new construction activity which thereby compounds local frustration. Houston's rents didn't grow at all in 3rd quarter 2026, and because of that stagnation, rent cuts today are now similar to their COVID-era low point (about 2% rent cuts year-over-year). Class A rent growth just returned this quarter, with prices climbing 1% year-over-year, the first annual increase the segment has seen in four quarters. Granted, Class B rents (down 1.9%) and Class C (down 5.4%) do highlight a story of deeper challenges elsewhere. Houston might be the biggest miss I've had in the past two years. One theory I tend to buy into in Houston is that single family demand poaches demand away from multifamily at a higher-than-usual pace. In fact, multifamily permits make up just 25% of total Houston MSA permitting on average. Only Cleveland, Memphis, Greensboro, Sacramento, Inland Empire, Las Vegas and Indianapolis see a higher skew toward single family. So essentially, Houston demand gets diluted by lots of housing supply (in turn, informing part of this metro's relative affordability). And here in the past year or two, demand has been even more ephemeral with immigration reform and energy sector ups-and-downs. items.title: Affordability Challenges Push New Home Sales Lower
items.description: Affordability Challenges Push New Home Sales Lower October 27, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments High mortgage rates and economic uncertainty continued to keep potential home buyers on the sidelines and constrain new home sales in September. New home sales declined from August and remained below year-ago levels, with year-to-date sales also lagging for 2025. Although builders have increasingly adjusted prices and offered incentives to attract buyers, elevated mortgage rates and ongoing affordability concerns continue to constrain sales activity. Sales of newly built single-family homes declined 0.6% in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000, following a downwardly revised August estimate, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and the U.S. Census Bureau . This represented a 5.3% decline from a year earlier. On a year-to-date basis, new home sales are down 2.9%. A new home sale is recorded when a contract is signed, or a deposit is accepted, regardless of the stage of construction. The seasonally adjusted annual rate reflects the pace of sales that would occur over a 12-month period if current conditions persist. New single-family home inventory in September was at 476,000 units and down 2.3% from a year ago. At the current sales pace, the months’ supply of new homes stood at an elevated 8.4 months, roughly unchanged from a year ago. A five- to six-month inventory level generally indicates a balanced market. Combined new and existing home inventory has edged higher in recent months, with the total months’ supply reaching 5.2 months. Inventory conditions in the existing home market have gradually improved in recent months. Moderating prices across both markets have helped support buyer demand amid ongoing affordability concerns. At the end of September, there were 111,000 completed, ready-to-occupy homes available for sale on a non-seasonally adjusted basis. Completed homes accounted for approximately one-quarter of total inventory, while homes under construction made up 53%. The remaining share of homes sold in September had not yet started construction at the time the sales contract was signed. New home prices showed mixed movement in September, reflecting changes in the composition of sales and continued builder incentives. The median new home sale price was $400,400, up 3.9% from August but down 3.9% compared to a year ago. Homes priced between $300,000 and $499,999 accounted for half of all new home sales, while 20% of sales were priced below $300,000, underscoring ongoing affordability challenges for entry-level buyers. The remaining 31% of sales were priced above $500,000. It is worth noting that the share of homes priced below $300,000 has increased since the beginning of the year, while the share priced over $500,000 has decreased. Regional performance was mixed in September. The Northeast posted the strongest monthly gain in sales, rising 28.0% from August, followed by the West, where sales increased 21.4%. In contrast, sales declined 6.6% in the South and 7.3% in the Midwest. Compared with September 2025, the Northeast recorded a 10.3% increase in new home sales, the only region to post an increase. Sales declined 0.7% in the South, 8.2% in the Midwest, and 17.4% in the West. On a year-to-date basis, regional trends were similarly uneven. New home sales increased 2.3% in the Northeast. items.title: Rocket posts $709M profit in Q3 despite tougher mortgage market
items.description: Rocket Companies on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of $709 million, reversing a loss from a year ago as the Detroit-based mortgage lender expanded revenue and gained market share in purchase and refinance lending. The company reported net income of $709 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a net loss of $124 million a year earlier and a second-quarter 2026 net income of $229 million. Net total revenue nearly doubled year over year to $3.28 billion, up from $1.7 billion, while adjusted revenue rose to $2.57 billion, up from $1.87 billion. Adjusted net income fell to $419 million from $441 million in Q2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA declined to $748 million from Q2's $766 million. Mortgage production also slowed, with closed origination volume falling to $43.6 billion, down from $49.1 billion. The sequential decline in adjusted earnings came as mortgage production slowed from the second quarter, even as the company reported a slightly higher gain-on-sale margin. Rocket chief financial officer Brian Brown anticipated the slowdown during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call, saying he expected Q3 to be “smaller than the second,” a contraction not seen in the industry since 2022. He cited rates above 6.8% and rising inflation expectations as key challenges. “Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” CEO Varun Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage , and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.” During the company's earnings call on Thursday afternoon, Krishna addressed the broader market. "Here's the truth about tough markets: They don't lie," he said. "They strip everything down to what's real. Who has the capital to keep investing? Whose model works in any cycle? Who can win their clients back? And who can move fast when it counts? This quarter did all of this." Brown said during the call that the company estimates its purchase market share approached 6.5% in Q3 2026, up from 6.2% in Q2 2026. Its refinance share reached 15.5%, compared with 14.3% from April through June. Mortgage production and servicing Rocket closed $43.6 billion in mortgage originations in the third quarter, down from $49.1 billion in Q2. Net rate-lock volume fell to $40.4 billion from $47 billion over the same period. The company’s total gain-on-sale margin edged up to 2.54% from 2.48% in Q2. Excluding correspondent lending , Rocket closed $33.5 billion in mortgage volume during the third quarter. Direct-to-consumer lending accounted for $24.6 billion, while wholesale channel Rocket Pro generated $9 billion. The correspondent channel contributed $10.1 billion in closed volume. Rocket’s mortgage servicing portfolio remained steady at about $2 trillion in unpaid principal balance across 9.1 million loans. The company sold mortgage servicing rights tied to $23 billion in unpaid principal balance during Q3, generating $379 million in proceeds. That was down from $53 billion in MSR sales and $795 million in proceeds in Q2. Rocket retained subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the servicing rights sold in the third quarter, compared with nearly 80% in Q2. Total liquidity rose to $11.4 billion at the end of Q3, up from $11.2 billion at the end of the prior quarter. The figure includes $2.7 billion in cash, $2.5 billion in undrawn credit lines and $6.2 billion in available servicing-rights and advance lines. Rocket said its combined servicing portfolio following the Mr. Cooper integration continued to support borrower recapture, with the company reaching its highest recapture levels to date. During Q3, Rocket continued to expand its use of artificial intelligence and its partnerships with real estate companies. The company said it pulled credit on nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer loan volume before borrowers spoke with a loan officer, compared with none a year earlier. Digital mortgage applications accounted for more than 40% of retail refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of nondigital leads. AI voice technology handled 65% of inbound servicing calls, resolving more than half without human assistance. Rocket also reported growth in its real estate partnerships. Redfin visitors who clicked to begin a mortgage transaction increased 50% year over year, while Redfin’s contribution to Rocket’s refinance leads more than doubled in Q3. Listings tied to its Compass partnership reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in Q2. The company said its testing indicated qualifying borrowers could save an average of $1,600 in closing costs. Rocket Pro launched Orbit in October , offering eligible purchase borrowers same-day conditional approval and a 12-business-day timeline to clear-to-close. The company also extended a Compass pricing credit through the end of 2026. The partnership had generated more than $3 billion in rate locks since February. items.title: Uptick for Non-Conventional Financing in 2025
items.description: Uptick for Non-Conventional Financing in 2025 October 26, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Nationwide, the share of non-conventional financing for new home sales accounted for 32.4% of the market, according to NAHB analysis of the 2025 Census Bureau Survey of Construction (SOC) data. This was 1.7 percentage points higher than the 2024 share of 30.7%. As in previous years, conventional financing dominated the market, accounting for 67.6% of sales, although this was down from 69.3% in 2024. Non-conventional forms of financing (as opposed to conventional mortgage loans) include loans insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), VA-backed loans, cash purchases, and other types of financing, such as financing through the Rural Housing Service, Habitat for Humanity, loans from individuals, or state- or local government mortgage-backed bonds. The reliance on non-conventional financing varied across the United States, with 43% of new home sales using non-conventional financing in the Pacific division, compared with just 18% of new single-family home sales in the Middle Atlantic division. Nationwide, cash purchases and FHA-backed loans each represented the largest shares of non-conventional financing for new home purchases, accounting for 13% of all new home sales. Meanwhile, VA-backed loans accounted for a 4% market share in 2025, while other financing accounted for 2%. Cash purchases led non-conventional financing in six of the nine Census divisions. The New England division recorded the highest share, where 32% of new home sales were cash purchases, followed by 20% in the East North Central division, 18% in the East South Central division, 15% in the Mountain division, 13% in the Middle Atlantic division, and 10% in the West North Central division. FHA-backed loans accounted for the largest share of non-conventional financing in the Pacific division, representing 25% of new home sales, followed by the West South Central division at 21%. In contrast, no new homes sold in the New England division used FHA-backed loans. VA-backed loans were most prevalent in the Mountain division, accounting for 9% of new home sales. Notably, in the New England and Middle Atlantic divisions, no homes were sold using VA-backed loans in 2025. Other financing, such as the Rural Housing Service, Habitat for Humanity, loans from individuals, and state- or local government mortgage-backed bonds, accounted for the largest share in the East South Central division, where it represented 4% of new home sales. items.title: PCE Inflation Accelerated in September
items.description: PCE Inflation Accelerated in September October 29, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge accelerated in September after holding at 3.0% for three consecutive months, complicating the Fed's path to its 2% target. Consumer spending continued to be pushed up by elevated energy prices rather than income growth, driving the personal saving rate to the lowest level in nearly four years. The headline Personal Consumption Expenditure (PCE) Price Index increased 3.6% in September from a year ago, the fastest pace since May, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis . The “core” PCE price index, which excludes food and energy, rose 3.1% over the past twelve months, following a 3.0% increase last month. Core PCE has remained at or above 3.0% since the start of the Iran conflict, suggesting inflation pressure persists even excluding volatile energy prices. Consumer spending rose 0.5% in September, while real spending, adjusted to remove inflation, remained unchanged. Meanwhile, personal income rose 0.2% in September. This growth was led by increases in compensation and government social benefits. Real disposable income—income adjusted for taxes and inflation—fell 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, personal income was 4.1% higher, and real (inflation-adjusted) disposable income was up 1.0%. With spending growth outpacing income growth, the personal saving rate fell to 3.8% in September, the lowest level since November 2022. items.title: Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data
items.description: Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data Published on October 26th, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data. Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low. Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday. Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future. items.title: U.S. Home-Sale Prices Just Fell for the First Time in 3 Years
items.description: U.S. Home-Sale Prices Just Fell for the First Time in 3 Years Published on October 29th, 2026 by Dana Anderson The median monthly mortgage payment is still sitting at its second-highest level on record, spooking would-be buyers. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending October 25: The median U.S. home-sale price has fallen for the first time in more than three years . The median home-sale price was $389,601, down 0.1% year over year. That marks the second straight week in which prices ticked down–it follows a 0.2% decline last week–after three straight years of increases. Homebuying demand fell to a new low. Pending home sales declined 1.8% from a week earlier to the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. For the third week in a row, pending sales declined in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metro areas. The typical homebuyer’s monthly payment hit its second-highest level on record. The median mortgage payment was $2,786, up 10.7% year over year to the highest level in our record except the prior week. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.32% , down from 7.4% a week earlier but still near a three-year high. Would-be sellers pulled back. New listings declined 0.6% from a week earlier to their lowest level since the start of the year as homeowners react to slow homebuying demand. Total supply is creeping up. The total number of homes for sale ticked up 0.3% from a week earlier. Even though new listings are falling, pending sales are falling more, keeping the pool of inventory partly filled. There are hundreds of thousands more home sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they’ve had in over a decade. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drift Lower, but Not Enough to Make Waiting Worthwhile
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drift Lower, but Not Enough to Make Waiting Worthwhile Mortgage rates may be edging down from their peak, but with home prices still climbing, waiting a year to buy will only trim a negligible $26 off a typical monthly payment. Written by Kara Ng on October 28, 2026 In short: Mortgage rates may be edging down from their peak, but with home prices still climbing, waiting a year to buy will only trim a negligible $26 off a typical monthly payment. Mortgage rates off peak but still elevated Mortgage rates continue to ease from their recent peak, though they remain significantly higher than a year ago. The Federal Reserve held rates steady in its October meeting, to allow more time to observe the impact of previous tightening. But markets expect an 80%+ chance of a hike in December. That hiking bias reflects persistent inflation issues. Shelter disinflation has effectively plateaued in the near-term, with new-lease rents having been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026. Meanwhile, the September Consumer Price Index report showed inflation running hotter than expected beyond energy prices. With inflation reluctant to budge, Zillow expects mortgage rates to ease only gradually, remaining at 7% or higher for the rest of 2026 and 6.5% or higher in 2027. What’s the impact on housing? Challenging affordability continues to weigh on the for-sale market. Newly pending sales, a leading indicator of future closings, fell 8.5% year over year in September . At the same time, rental demand skyrocketed, with rental engagement per listing growing 19.2% compared to last year, as elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead. Still, for a buyer who has decided to purchase a home, but is questioning when, here is the tradeoff. Borrowing costs are expected to ease, but only slightly. Home values, meanwhile, are expected to rise modestly nationwide, offsetting some of the savings from lower rates. Put together, those forecasts suggest waiting a year would shave just $26 off the monthly mortgage payment compared with buying today. In other words, delaying doesn’t gain much. items.title: Homeownership Rate Rises to 65.5%
items.description: Homeownership Rate Rises to 65.5% October 28, 2026 Na Zhao No Comments The latest homeownership rate reached 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Census’s Housing Vacancy Survey (HVS). While this was a modest quarterly increase, the broader picture continues to reflect significant affordability challenges. With mortgage interest rates remaining elevated, and housing supply still tight, housing affordability is at a multidecade low. Compared to the peak of 69.2% in 2004, the homeownership rate is currently 3.7 percentage points lower and remains below the 25-year average rate of 66.3%. Compared to the previous year, homeownership rates decreased in three age groups. Householders aged 35-44 experienced the largest drop, declining by 1 percentage point from 61.1% to 60.1%. Among younger households, the homeownership rate for those under 35 decreased 0.9 percentage points to 36.6% in the third quarter of 2026. This age group is particularly sensitive to mortgage rates and the inventory of entry-level homes. The 55-64 age group saw a 0.6 percentage point decrease, declining from 76% to 75.4%. Homeownership rates for householders ages 65 years and over inched up by 1.2 percentage points over the same time, followed by 0.4 percentage point increase for 45-54 age group The national rental vacancy rate inched up to 7.6% for the third quarter of 2026, on a steadily increasing trend since 2023. Meanwhile, the homeowner vacancy rate stayed at 1.2%. The upticks in both homeowner and rental vacancy rate signal an increase in the existing home supply . The housing stock-based HVS revealed that the total number of households increased to 134 million in the third quarter of 2026 from 133.2 million a year ago. This increase was driven by both owner and renter household growth. items.title: Despite pausing rate hikes, ‘inflation is too high’: Fed chair
items.description: An article from Despite pausing rate hikes, ‘inflation is too high’: Fed chair The news didn’t surprise apartment investors, who tuned in for signals indicating future rate increases. Published Oct. 28, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images As expected, the Federal Open Market Committee held interest rates steady on Wednesday, following its two-day October meeting. Despite two dissenters who voted to raise the federal funds rate target range by 0.25 percentage points, the FOMC kept it at 3.75% to 4%. For the apartment industry, the news was welcome after the FOMC hiked the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points in September. “Expectations are clearly for the Fed to stand pat, which helps,” Jeff Brown, CEO and co-founder at T2 Capital Management, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments ahead of the Fed’s announcement. In a press conference following today's announcement, Kevin Warsh, chair of the Federal Reserve, said the goal was to deliver price stability. He also announced a change to the Fed’s 2028 schedule. It will still meet eight times, but only six will set policy. “As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said. “That's good news. But inflation is too high.” Multiple multifamily owners and investors said they would watch the announcement closely, even if they don’t expect relief anytime soon. Instead, they wanted to understand what could be coming late in the year and in 2027. Trickle-down effect After multiple rate cuts in 2025 , the Fed held rates steady before raising them in September, a move that affected the multifamily market. While “cap rates have moved out since the September meeting,” sellers are slow to accept it, said Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser said. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die. I’d expect volume to stay thin through year-end, especially if the Fed signals a December hike.” Smita Garg, principal of investments and asset management at apartment owner and manager SKG Capital, said her firm was closely watching the Fed’s announcement because it “was actively evaluating and executing transactions where today’s cost of capital has a direct impact on pricing and returns.” “Higher borrowing costs continue to make multifamily transactions more difficult to execute,” Garg told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. “Financing costs directly affect what buyers can pay while still achieving appropriate returns, and sellers have not always adjusted expectations to the same degree. That disconnect continues to limit transaction volume.” Forward outlook In its statement, the Federal Reserve said economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, and domestic spending has been resilient, despite geopolitical uncertainty. “Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust,” Warsh said. “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.” Financial and credit conditions have tightened for some businesses and households after September’s rate hike, according to Warsh. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight,” Warsh said. “But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.” Still, Warsh said multiple times that inflation remains elevated. “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” he said. Warsh said more information is needed before the Fed decides to raise rates again, noting that indicators like oil futures were continuing to rise. “Ensuring price stability … quashing inflation, is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar,” Warsh said. “[The] same way, it's not about some isolated data point.” Tone matters For apartment observers, Warsh’s comments seemed to matter more than the Fed’s decision. Chesser wasn’t surprised by the rate pause, but he wanted to know what comes later. “After September’s hike, the market is trying to read whether another one comes in December, and Chair Warsh’s tone will move the 10-year Treasury more than the decision itself,” Chesser said. “That matters for us because most apartment debt is priced off Treasuries, not the Fed funds rate.” Like Chesser, Garg was also watching Wednesday’s announcement to decipher the Fed’s roadmap into 2027. “For us, the more important question is not necessarily this week’s decision, but the direction of rates over the next six to 12 months,” Garg said. “Greater visibility around the rate path would help bring more certainty back to underwriting and ultimately help buyers and sellers close the gap on pricing.” Regardless, some firms are preparing for higher rates to stick around. “I don't know that we're going to see material drops in rates over the near term,” Greg Cavanaugh, senior vice president of development for the mid-Atlantic region at Bainbridge, told Multifamily Dive. Even with Wednesday’s announcement and Warsh's comments, Chris Nebenzahl, CBRE's Americas head of multifamily research, said the market might not have a clear picture for a few more months. "Greater clarity around the rate outlook should materialize in early 2027, helping bring buyers and sellers back together, improving price discovery and supporting higher transaction volume as investors gain confidence in the market,” he said in emailed comments.
